executiveSummary: A Saturday class for home bakers on why dough rises: yeast makes the gas, gluten holds it, and warmth sets the pace, so a baker who reads the dough rather than the clock controls the loaf.

slides.slideTitle: Why your bread rises, and why it sometimes doesn't
slides.subtitle: Saturday baking class · Eastside Library · Week 3
slides.speakerNotes:
- Welcome back. Last week three of you brought in loaves you called bricks.
- Today we find out why, and it is not your recipe.

slides.slideTitle: A dense loaf is almost always a timing problem
keyBullets: Same flour, same recipe, same oven: two hours apart
slides.speakerNotes:
- Here is the experiment I ran on Thursday. One dough, split in two.
- I baked half after two hours and half after four. The first was a brick. The second was the loaf you wanted.
- Nothing changed but time.

slides.slideTitle: Yeast eats the sugar in flour and breathes out the gas that lifts the loaf
keyBullets: Yeast: a single-celled fungus
It turns sugar into carbon dioxide and a little alcohol
slides.speakerNotes:
- Yeast is alive, and it is hungry.
- It eats the sugars in flour and gives off carbon dioxide. Those bubbles are your rise.
- The alcohol bakes off. It leaves some flavor behind.

slides.slideTitle: Gluten is the net that holds the gas in
keyBullets: Water and flour proteins make gluten
Kneading lines the strands up
A strong net holds the bubbles; a weak one lets them out
slides.speakerNotes:
- Gas alone does nothing if it escapes.
- Gluten forms when flour meets water, and kneading lines it up into a stretchy net.
- Pull a piece of your dough thin. If light shows through without tearing, the net is ready.

slides.slideTitle: Warmth sets the pace: a few degrees changes the rise by hours
keyBullets: Kitchen at 18°C: about 4 hours
Kitchen at 26°C: about 2 hours
slides.speakerNotes:
- Yeast works faster when it is warm.
- In a cool winter kitchen, a rise that the recipe calls two hours takes four.
- That is where most bricks come from: the recipe was written in someone else's warmer kitchen.

slides.slideTitle: The poke test tells you when the dough is ready
keyBullets: Flour a finger and press it in a centimeter
Springs back fast: wait
Springs back slowly and leaves a dent: bake
Stays down: it went too far
slides.speakerNotes:
- So stop watching the clock and watch the dough.
- Press it gently. If it springs right back, the net is still tight, give it time.
- A slow spring with a small dent means bake now. Let's each try it on the bowls in front of you.

slides.slideTitle: Shape gently, so the gas you waited for stays in
keyBullets: Fold, don't punch
Tuck the edges under to tighten the skin
slides.speakerNotes:
- You waited hours for those bubbles. Don't punch them out.
- Fold the dough over itself and tuck the edges under. The tight skin helps the loaf stand up in the oven.

slides.slideTitle: In a cold kitchen, give it more time, not more yeast
keyBullets: More yeast: a fast rise, a flat taste
More time: the rise you want, and the flavor with it
slides.speakerNotes:
- The tempting fix is more yeast. It works, but the loaf tastes of nothing.
- Flavor comes from time. In a cold kitchen, let it go an extra hour or two, or put it in the oven with only the light on.

keyBullets: A: tight crumb, small holes, heavy
B: big holes near the top, flat, a little sour
C: even holes, domed, springy
slides.speakerNotes:
- Look at the three photos on your handout.
- Take a moment. The answer is B: the net gave out, the gas escaped up top, and it slumped.
- A rose too little. C is the one we are after.

slides.slideTitle: Control the time and the temperature, and you control the loaf
slides.subtitle: Bring your loaf next Saturday
keyBullets: This week: bake one loaf and change only the rise time
slides.speakerNotes:
- That is the whole idea: the yeast makes the gas, the gluten holds it, and you set the pace with time and warmth.
- Bake one loaf this week and change only how long it rises. Bring it, or a photo, next Saturday.
slides.intent: Land the idea and set homework
